output:
You feel awful. Your throat hurts, your nose runs, and you want something to fix it. Antibiotics feel like the obvious answer, because they cleared up that chest infection last winter. But against a cold they do nothing at all, and the reason comes down to what is actually making you ill.

Colds are caused by viruses. Antibiotics are built to kill bacteria. These are two completely different kinds of thing.

Bacteria are living cells. They have their own outer walls, their own machinery for building proteins, their own way of multiplying. Antibiotics work by sabotaging that machinery. Some punch holes in the cell wall. Others jam the protein factory so the bacterium cannot grow or divide.

Viruses have almost none of that equipment. A virus is little more than a scrap of genetic instructions in a protective coat. It cannot reproduce on its own. It breaks into one of your cells and hijacks that cell's machinery to make copies of itself. There is no bacterial wall to puncture, no bacterial factory to jam.

Picture a key cut precisely for one lock. Hand it to someone standing in front of a different door, and the quality of the key is irrelevant. It simply does not fit.

Taking them anyway is not harmless. You may get diarrhoea or a rash, and you kill off useful bacteria in your gut. Worse, the bacteria that survive repeated exposure learn to shrug antibiotics off. That is how resistance spreads, and it makes future infections harder to treat for everyone.

A cold clears on its own in a week or so, while your immune system does the work. Rest, fluids and painkillers ease the symptoms in the meantime.

In short, antibiotics target bacteria, and a cold is a virus — the wrong weapon for the wrong enemy.
